summary: We designed Mars Station for the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. In this browser game for ages 7–12, players lead five crewmates through 15 Martian days and split limited power among life support, radiation protection, food production, and communications. Historical NASA space weather records inform the scenarios. Players see how one day’s decisions affect crew safety and research later in the mission.
details:
How does it work?

You are the captain of a Mars base. You have 15 sols (martian days) to keep 5 crew members safe and send scientific research to Earth before the return ship arrives. Every sol starts with a sol briefing. You assign the available solar power, handle the event for the sol, and see how it affected supplies and crew health. If you have power to your antenna, then you can send one message to Earth that evening. Requests for help and science reports are sent in the same time slot and you receive a reply the next morning. Decisions have consequences for the hull of your space station too. A damaged hull illustrates this. If a repair crew has to venture outside, they will be exposed to radiation, but keep them inside, and the station will lose resources overnight. The captain’s report gives reflection of how your decisions affected the crew and the science sent to Earth. The success of the mission depends on the safety of the crew and the results of the scientific work. Constantly changing weather conditions allow you to rethink your tactics during your mission.

If the hull is damaged during a radiation warning, the player should decide whether to repair it right away by sending someone from the crew or not sending anyone. Sending someone from the crew exposes them to radiation and also distracts them from their job. If the player decides to not send anyone, the station will lose air overnight. At the end, the captain's report shows how the choices that the player made affected crew safety and how much research was delivered to Earth. If the player keeps the crew safe and completes the science mission, the player earns the highest rating.


Why it matters?
It matters because the challenge forces students to experience how their decisions affect the mission. As a result, they can experience how trade-offs shape a space mission. They can try the same scenario again at the same difficulty, use a new strategy, and explain how their new mission ended differently. We made each session take about 15 minutes. This way, teachers can use it for a short activity at the end of a class. Families can play together at home.

Benefits and the intented impact

Our game gives the opportunity for kids age 7-12 to practice planning ahead, and prioritize resources in complex space conditions. We designed the game for a 15-minute session that runs in browser without sign-in. After a lost mission the debrief shows what went wrong so that children can try again instead of giving up


Tools used

The alpha build is written in TypeScript. The UI uses React, the project is built with Vite, and the tests run on Vitest.

NASA Image and Video Library —real photos of Mars and the ISS for the album cards
